question.text: An exporter with USD receivables sells a USDINR call option at strike Rs 85 for Rs 0.60 when spot is Rs 84. This is equivalent to which equity strategy?

answer.text: Covered call — the exporter owns the underlying (USD receivables) and writes a call to earn premium income, giving up upside above Rs 85
Protective put — because it protects the export revenue
Long straddle — because the exporter is taking a volatility position
Naked call writing — because the exporter doesn't own any underlying

explanation.text: The Logic: The exporter has a natural long USD position from the receivable. Selling a USDINR call mirrors an equity covered call: the existing underlying exposure backs the short option. If USDINR settles above Rs 85 on the exercise date, the short call has a negative cash payoff equal to (settlement − 85) per USD, which offsets the gain the exporter would otherwise have made on the USD receivable above Rs 85 — capping the effective realised rate near Rs 85 plus the Rs 0.60 premium received. If USDINR stays below Rs 85, the call lapses and the exporter keeps the full premium. The Trap: It is not naked call writing because the exporter has the underlying USD receivable. It is not a protective put (which would require buying a put). Not a straddle (only one option leg). Note: Currency option exercise on the Indian exchanges is cash-settled in INR on T+2, not via physical delivery of USD. The "covered" nature of the position comes from the offsetting USD receivable cash flow, not from delivering dollars into the option contract.
